insider_note: Whenever the numerator is linear and the denominator is a square root of a quadratic, write the numerator as A times the quadratic's derivative plus a leftover constant B — the A-part always integrates to 2√(quadratic), no matter what the quadratic is.

steps.label: Write the numerator as A·Dr′ + B and solve for A, B
steps.why: A linear numerator over a square root ALWAYS splits this way — matching the x-coefficient fixes A first, then the constant term fixes B from A.
common_mistakes: Matching the constant term first, which needs A already known and leads to circular working.
Sign slip: −2A+B=5 with A=1 gives B=7, not B=3.
steps.memory_tip: Match the x-coefficient FIRST to get A; the constant equation then gives B directly.

steps.label: Substitute back and split the integral
steps.why: The A-part is an f′(x)/√f(x) form, a standard result equal to 2√f(x) — it needs no completing the square at all, unlike the leftover B-part.
common_mistakes: Trying to complete the square on the WHOLE numerator 2x+5 instead of splitting it into the A and B pieces first.
Missing the factor of 2 in ∫f′(x)/√f(x) dx = 2√f(x), writing just √f(x).
steps.memory_tip: ∫f′/√f dx = 2√f — always a factor of 2, easy to drop by habit.

steps.label: Complete the square under the root
steps.why: This is now a sum of squares under the root, (x−1)²+3² — the exact shape the standard ∫dx/√(x²+a²) = sinh⁻¹(x/a) formula needs.
common_mistakes: Not recognising 9 = 3² and instead leaving it as a bare constant.

steps.label: Apply the standard sinh⁻¹ form for the final answer
steps.why: Substituting x → (x−1) and a=3 into the standard sinh⁻¹ formula, then multiplying by the leftover B=7, gives the second half of the final answer.
common_mistakes: Using Sin⁻¹ (bounded, for a²−x² under the root) instead of Sinh⁻¹ (unbounded, for x²+a² under the root) — the two look alike but are different functions.
Forgetting to multiply the sinh⁻¹ term by B=7.
steps.memory_tip: x²+a² under a root ⇒ Sinh⁻¹ (hyperbolic); a²−x² under a root ⇒ Sin⁻¹ (circular) — different letter cases matter here.
